I think trying to track how much work AI can do autonomously is critical, and this is a useful counter to some of the most audacious claims about the state of autonomous AI research. But I do want to note that the focus on research tasks at the most advanced AI research organizations on the planet also runs the risk of substantially underestimating what AI can already do in terms of economically valuable tasks. Its worth separating the two (and I don't think Ramez is claiming they are not seperated). Most work is not frontier AI research, and there AI can be tremendously successful. Epoch's MirrorCode results, for example, show AI autonomously reimplementing software that the researchers estimate would take a humans 2-17 weeks. This is well-specified work, so it has very different boundary conditions. Plus, in the real world, some human intervention is fine (in my mind, vastly preferrable to no human role for a variety of reasons). Occasional guidance can still leave you with enormous productivity gains, even if that doesn’t satisfy the requirements for fully autonomous AI research. And even in the case of AI research, the same OpenAI report includes researchers estimating that a month of their team’s work would have taken three months without coding agents, on average. In short, RSI/AI-driven research progress may not tightly couple with progress on economically valuable tasks, and the variance and range on those tasks are less well understood. IMPORTANT NOTE: EBM are often presented as a particular form of probabilistic models. This is a very common misunderstanding. EBMs are *MORE GENERAL* than probabilistic models. Probabilistic models are a special case of EBMs in which: 1. Energies can be turned into a probabilities through the Gibbs distribution. That requires a convergent and computable partition function! 2. The loss function has a probabilistic interpretation, e.g. negative likelihood. But there is whole world of EBMs that are NOT probabilistic: they require no partition function or normalization, and they can be trained with lots of loss functions that have no probabilistic interpretation.

That's the essence of my Deep Learning course at NYU for the past 20 years or so. Everything can be understood within the unified framework of energy-based models, including classification, regression, structured prediction, unsupervised and self-supervised learning (clustering, auto-encoders, denoising AE, variational AE, Siamese nets, joint embedding, JEPA, diffusion models,...). Yet another amazing JEPA paper, and it's also supervised by Yann LeCun! "The Content–Geometry Tradeoff in World Models: When JEPA Learns Latent Maps" JEPA world models have a tradeoff where they can learn a smooth map for navigation, but would lose track of objects they need to interact with. So this paper introduces Slow SVReg, which helps the model learn a smoother map of its environment while preserving important details, such as the positions of objects that change slowly. On difficult first-person maze navigation, Slow SVReg improves planning success from 21.2% to 92.9% compared to a standard stop-gradient baseline. On the PushT manipulation task, success increases from 44.0% to 87.3%. https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.jepa-latent-maps-content-geometry

Software engineering and research have changed significantly for me. A big mistake I made early on was trying to automate everything. Instead of trying to automate everything at once with a bunch of silly and subjective skills, I now spend most of my time helping my coding and research agents write better code and explore novel research ideas. That's right! I am more involved. I think this approach works best today, given the current state of coding agents. Not only for coding but for researching as well. This process has resulted in good patterns codified as loops. Loops involve automations, but they also include clear, intentional steps you can keep refining to remove jaggedness. I continually strengthen my loops through verifiers, deterministic steps, context formatting and awareness, memory systems, and evals that steer quality and robustness. So I agree with other great engineering leaders that our job has fundamentally changed. It's not about using LLMs to help us write code. It's helping the LLM write code better and faster. That's where those loops come into play. This has significantly reduced error rates and allowed me to expand and scale with coding agents in unbelievable ways. Something I naively expected from my initial, silly, outdated automations. It feels contradictory at first, since we treat coding agents as solve-it-all intelligence, but it's a system like other traditional systems that requires careful attention to unlock its benefits. Like my other peers, I believe we are in the early innings. There are more core primitives, interfaces, and experiences to build. For example, we still haven't fully figured out agent swarms. Coding agents only really started to take off around this time last year. It's unbelievable how much has changed since then. To be better prepared for what's coming next year, I continue to advocate for gaining deeper knowledge and developing mastery and expertise in your domain. That will continue to matter.

Can an AI agent settle an open physics question with a machine-checked proof? This new paper from the University of Tübingen and Google DeepMind shows that it can. The question comes from quantum optics. Physicists wanted to know whether high-dimensional GHZ states, a kind of entangled photon state, can be built with only linear optics and pair sources. The authors first raised it in 2017. The answer is no. For any even number of photons from 4 upward, with at least as many dimensions as photons, the construction is impossible. AlphaProof Nexus found the proof. It searches for formal proofs in Lean, combining frontier language models with feedback from the Lean compiler. Because the proof is formal, a computer verifies it. The authors then worked out what the proof means physically and explained it in the paper. This is one of the clearest recent examples of formal proof search producing a new result outside pure math. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26300 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/a-tensor-algebraic-no-go-theorem-for-high-dimensional-photonic-greenberger-horne-2611.26300

Can coding agents build better RAG systems than the best published human designs? AutoRAGBench gives an agent nine RAG development tasks to measure this. There is no starter code and no suggested approach. The agent gets six hours and one H800 GPU to analyze the data, build a pipeline, and refine it from experiments. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI averages 56.1. The composite human baseline, which takes the best published method on each task, averages 44.4. When the agent starts from a human-designed system instead of from scratch, it adds 16.6 points on average across seven tasks. The paper compares nine agent setups and also studies how each one's development process unfolds over the six hours. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25582 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/autoragbench-a-benchmark-for-llm-agents-automating-rag-system-development-2611.25582
